name: Clark Stanley's Snake Oil Liniment

card.summary: A rattlesnake-oil rub marketed in the late 1800s for aches and pains; recovery-minded users applied liniments to ease sore muscles and joints, and its 1916-17 analysis made it a famous case study.
card.note: Historical product; analysis found mineral oil, fat, capsaicin and turpentine.

quick.overview:
Clark Stanley's Snake Oil Liniment was a rub sold by the self-styled "Rattlesnake King" Clark Stanley. It was positioned as a remedy for aches and pains, the kind of topical product people reach for to feel looser and recover between efforts.

A US Bureau of Chemistry examination, dated 1916 or 1917 depending on the source, found mineral oil, a fat, capsaicin from chili peppers and turpentine, and Stanley was fined $20 [1]. The case helped make "snake oil" a term for dubious remedies.
quick.how: It was a topical liniment rubbed onto sore areas, sold at medicine shows and by mail. It is no longer sold, though the capsaicin-and-oil approach continues in modern warming rubs.
quick.risks: Capsaicin and turpentine can irritate skin. The product was found to lack the snake oil its marketing claimed, and the case is cited in discussion of the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906.

lead: Clark Stanley's Snake Oil Liniment was a patent liniment sold by Clark Stanley, an herbalist born about 1854 who billed himself the "Rattlesnake King" [1]. Stanley said he learned the remedy from a Hopi medicine man in Arizona after 1879 [1].

He drew attention at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, and produced the liniment in Massachusetts and Rhode Island [1]. A federal examination found mineral oil, a fatty material probably from beef, capsaicin and turpentine, and he was fined $20 [1].

For readers focused on recovery, liniments of this type are rubbed onto sore muscles and joints for warming relief so that people can resume training sooner; the capsaicin component is a recognized counterirritant in modern rubs.

chain: Rub liniment on sore muscles or joints
angle.text: It was marketed for aches and pains. Users rubbed it on sore areas, and the effect that remains traceable in the analysis is a warming, counterirritant sensation from capsaicin.

paras: Stanley's account of Hopi training from 1879 was his own marketing story [1]. He sold at Western medicine shows with help from a Boston druggist and later manufactured in Beverly, Massachusetts and Providence, Rhode Island [1].
Wikipedia's lead dates exposure to 1916 while the body cites a 1917 Bureau of Chemistry publication; the fine followed passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 [1].
Stanley is credited with popularizing the phrase "snake oil salesman," which became shorthand for ineffective products sold as cures [1].
